newsitem.title: ALBANIA: U.S. turns heat on Albania, Europe lukewarm.
newsitem.headline: U.S. turns heat on Albania, Europe lukewarm.

text.p: President Sali Berisha is coming under growing international pressure to shore up democracy in Albania with the United States pressing hardest for fresh general elections to halt a spiral of nationwide unrest.
Washington once again appears to be taking the lead to secure stability in the Balkan region after bringing the Bosnian war to an end through the U.S.-brokered Dayton accords.

The United States has over the past nine months repeatedly insisted on early elections after it described last May's nationwide polls as seriously flawed and accompanied by serious human rights abuses.
Berisha's right-wing Democratic Party almost swept the board in the elections, winning 122 of 140 parliamentary seats.

The U.S. State Department on Tuesday expressed concern over unrest sparked by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes, the decision by authorities to prevent peaceful protest and the reported beatings of opposition supporters and journalists.

European Union foreign ministers on Monday criticised the Albanian government for the violence used to crush the protests but they made no mention of the government's democratic record, merely advising Tirana to stick to democratic principles if it wants to receive further EU aid.

European governments have made little public comment on last year's election, even though the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), of which all 15 EU states are members, issued a critical report citing incidents of intimidation, ballot rigging and election law violations.
Despite its tough words, the report was largely watered down and Europeans within the OSCE have been lukewarm towards any further initiative on Albania, diplomatic sources said.
The EU ministers this week were clearly warning Albania it was being watched, but Berisha has been touting their statement as an expression of support for his administration.
"Our alternative has the full support of the European Union," Berisha told a rally a day after the EU meeting.
"European morbidezza (weakness)" read the headline on a commentary by the independent daily Koha Jone on Wednesday.
"(The) decision of the meeting of EU ministers not to ask for snap elections was considered by most Albanians as a political mascarade," the commentary said.
"Europe which showed itself to be impotent before the Bosnian conflict can not afford to have another...which might very well turn out to be a powder keg for the entire Balkan region," it added.
No-one has suggested that unrest in Albania could be coupled with Belgrade's tightening of the screws on ethnic Albanians in Kosovo or protests over the use of Albanian in Macedonian high schools.
While discontent among Albanians in the region does exist and could be tapped, there appears to be little appetite in Tirana for any adventure abroad to divert attention at home.
Current rights in Albania are undoubtedly an improvement on the oppressive Stalinist regime toppled in 1990 but the U.S. State Department said the government's human rights record worsened in 1996.
"The flawed May elections, coming at a time of further government pressure on the judiciary and the press were major steps backwards for democracy," its human rights report said.
Washington is deeply disillusioned with Berisha who was once regarded as a serious ally in a region wracked by war.
Berisha in turn allowed unmanned U.S. spy planes monitoring Bosnia to be stationed in Albania and invited U.S. troops to train in northern mountains.
But warm relations began to freeze rapidly after last year's polls.
"Washington was disappointed after investing so much time in Albania. It really felt it could do some good in what was communist Europe's most oppressed country," one Western diplomat said.

"President Berisha needs to pass a constitution as soon as possible and that would give him the opportunity to hold early elections. It's the only way to win back respect from the West," the diplomat said.
Berisha must seek a fresh five-year term in a parliamentary vote by March 9 but his re-election appears in little doubt with his Democrats holding 87 percent of seats.
